title: DATect: ML Algal Bloom Forecasts
description:
**Domoic acid** is a neurotoxin from harmful algal blooms off the Pacific Coast. When levels spike, fisheries close and the toxin can sicken people and sea lions, but managers usually only find out *after* it's already in the food web. DATect predicts those spikes a week out.

## What feeds a forecast

The model draws on 21 years of data: satellite ocean color, temperature, and plankton fluorescence (NASA `MODIS`); climate signals like PDO, ONI, and BEUTI upwelling; river streamflow; and measured toxin samples from 10 sites across Washington and Oregon. I line everything up into weekly series and train an `XGBoost` model to predict next week's toxin level, either a number (regression) or a risk tier of Low, Moderate, High, or Extreme (classification).

## Keeping it honest

It's easy to build a forecast that cheats. Let a model peek at data it wouldn't actually have yet and it looks brilliant in testing, then falls apart in production. DATect treats satellite data as arriving 7 days late and climate indices 2 months late, matching their real reporting lags, and splits the data by time instead of shuffling it. The model always trains on the past and gets tested on the future, so the score you see is close to what you'd get forecasting blind.

## Results

Under that strict temporal holdout, DATect hits an **R² of 0.315** and catches **85.9% of real toxin spikes**, about **434% better** than the 'next week looks like this week' persistence baseline managers lean on now.

title: DATect: Ocean Anomaly Detection
description:
Most forecasting models watch one monitoring site at a time. **Ocean Anomaly Detection (OAD)** flips that around: it learns what a healthy coastal ocean usually looks like, then flags the moment that picture starts to fall apart.

## Learning 'normal'

OAD is a **3D convolutional autoencoder**, a network that squeezes satellite imagery of the whole coastal ocean down to a compact code and rebuilds it. After training on 22 years of four-channel `MODIS` imagery (chlorophyll, sea-surface temperature, fluorescence, and related ocean-color bands), it gets good enough at reconstructing normal conditions that anything it *can't* rebuild cleanly jumps out, often the first visible hint of a developing bloom.

## The hard part

Satellite imagery is full of holes; clouds and sensor gaps leave missing pixels scattered across every image. OAD uses **masked convolutions** so the network skips those gaps instead of inventing values to fill them. It also works in 3D, across latitude, longitude, and time, so it can read how a region changes over a span rather than how it looks in a single frame.

## How it held up

Across a range of lead times, OAD was the **only method to keep a positive R² at a 7-day lead**. It still carried real signal a full week out, where simpler approaches had already washed into noise.

title: DATect: Full-Stack Cloud Application
description:
This is the web app that gets DATect in front of the fishery managers and researchers who actually need the forecasts. It's a **React + FastAPI** app running on **Google Cloud**.

## The dashboard

Pick a site and you get next week's prediction with bootstrap confidence intervals, the `XGBoost` features behind it, and a plain-language risk readout (Low, Moderate, High, or Extreme). You can switch between regression for continuous μg/g values and classification for risk tiers.

## A track record you can check

A retrospective mode replays 500+ past forecasts as predicted-vs-actual scatter plots and time series, with full per-site and per-class metrics (R², MAE, F1, accuracy). You can size up the model's history before trusting next week's number.

## Digging into the data

The historical analysis page has correlation heatmaps, Sobol sensitivity indices, domoic-acid-vs-Pseudo-nitzschia comparisons, waterfall plots, spectral analysis, and an interactive Pacific Coast site map. Everything renders as **Plotly.js** charts you can hover, filter by site, and export, all inside a responsive **Tailwind CSS** layout.

title: DATect: Research Awards
description:
**DATect** picked up recognition at two national science competitions.

## The awards

I won a **2024 ISEF Grand Award** at the International Science and Engineering Fair, the world's largest pre-college science competition, and was named a **2025 Regeneron Science Talent Search Scholar**, STS being the oldest science competition in the U.S.

## What it was for

Both came out of the domoic-acid forecasting work behind DATect: a leak-free machine-learning pipeline that predicts toxic algal blooms along the Pacific Coast about a week before they hit.

title: Geo-Aware Species Recognition
description:
Two birds can look nearly identical in a photo, but where the photo was taken often settles which species it actually is. This work builds species classifiers that combine **what the camera sees** with **where you are**, and runs the whole thing on a phone in under 50 milliseconds.

## Making vision and geography speak the same language

Image models and geospatial models don't normally share a vocabulary. I align **GeoTessera** location embeddings (a learned numeric fingerprint for any point on Earth) with **BioCLIP2** image embeddings so a place and a photo land in the same space, which lets location count as real evidence for which species is plausible.

## Adapting without retraining

The classifier runs a small **MobileViT** vision backbone steered by lightweight **adapter** and **FiLM** layers. Rather than retraining a whole network for each region, those small modules nudge the model using the location embedding, which is cheap to train and easy to extend to a new area.

## Built for the edge

Compiled to **Core ML**, it runs on the **Apple Neural Engine** in under 50 ms. Identification happens offline, in the field, with no server round-trip, so it feels instant in a live camera view.

title: Snow Crab Behavior Tracking
description:
Snow crab get sorted by the millions aboard Bering Sea fishing vessels, and how they move on the sorting table says a lot about which handling setups stress them least. This project turns overhead tank video into quantitative behavior data.

## Annotating the video

Every crab in every frame gets labeled in **CVAT** with a bounding box around the body plus an **orientation skeleton** of two keypoints, one for the head and one for the tail, so the data captures both where a crab is and which way it's facing. Annotations export in **Datumaro** format and feed a pipeline that stitches the per-frame labels into continuous trajectories.

## Getting orientation right

I built the **orientation scoring** that grades how well a predicted heading matches the truth. A crab's heading is directed, so mixing up head and tail counts as a full 180° error, and the metric has to punish those flips correctly. I also wrote the **inter-annotator agreement** analysis, which checks whether two people labeling the same clip actually agree, and that's what tells you the labels are worth trusting.

## From tracks to behavior

Further down the pipeline, the trajectories feed **escape-attempt detection** and a **correlated random walk** model of how crabs explore the tank. That's where the raw video becomes the step-length and turning-angle distributions biologists use to compare treatments.

title: ZAP-HD Fusion Logbook
description:
**ZAP-HD** is a sheared-flow Z-pinch fusion experiment at the University of Washington. The logbook researchers use to record and review every shot was an aging **PHP 4** app on Apache and Ubuntu 18.04, with raw SQL wired straight into the pages. I rebuilt it from scratch.

## The new stack

A **SvelteKit + TypeScript** frontend talks to a **FastAPI** backend over **PostgreSQL**, with **Pydantic** validating every request and response. TypeScript gives the logbook a fast, type-safe UI, and the Python API keeps the data model strict and self-documenting.

## Logging in with UW NetID

Auth is **JWT**-based and tied into UW NetID single sign-on. Getting there meant migrating the old **CAS** flow to **SAML 2.0** against UW's **Shibboleth** identity provider, so people's existing university accounts just work without a separate password.

## Shipping it securely

`nginx` terminates **TLS on port 443** with an InCommon certificate, the SvelteKit (Node, :3000) and FastAPI (:8081) services run under `systemd`, and deploys go out over SSH deploy keys. It lives at zaphd-logbook.aa.uw.edu.

title: CodeGraph
description:
**CodeGraph** was our **DubHacks 2025** hackathon project: a tool that turns a codebase into an explorable knowledge graph, so a team can see how their code, people, and history fit together without opening files one at a time.

## What the graph shows

Paste a GitHub repo URL, CodeGraph analyzes it, and you get an interactive, Obsidian-style graph: nodes for files, functions, contributors, and events, with edges for the relationships between them like dependencies, code reviews, and authorship. From the graph you can read who owns what, what depends on what, and where a team's knowledge is concentrated.

## How it's wired

It's an **Atlassian Forge** app that runs inside **Jira Cloud** project pages, so the graph sits where the team already works. A **Gemini**-powered layer pulls out the relationships, an **MCP** server connects the model to repository data, and **Cytoscape.js** draws the graph in a **React** front end.

title: Portfolio Website
description:
**This is that site.** A portfolio with no framework behind it, just **HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript** served from **GitHub Pages**.

## The desk

Projects sit on a draggable 'desk' of cards you can grab, throw, and watch collide, run by a little physics loop I wrote by hand. A cat trails your cursor, confetti fires when you open a project, and the card edges have a hand-drawn 'squigglevision' wobble made by animating an SVG turbulence filter. Every card comes from one `projects.json` file, so adding a project is a data edit instead of a code change. The animated intro was inspired by Hyperplexed's *Award Winning Animation With Only 20 Lines Of CSS?*

## Hidden easter eggs

Hit the backtick key and a fake terminal opens that runs some genuinely real things in the browser: **Conway's Game of Life** and a zoomable **Mandelbrot set** drawn as live ASCII, a `dig` command that does real **DNS-over-HTTPS** lookups, an `ip` command that geolocates your connection, a `mine` command that runs actual **SHA-256 proof-of-work** in a **Web Worker** so the page never freezes, and a `synth` command that plays a **Web Audio** chiptune with a live frequency spectrum. Open the site in two tabs and the cursors find each other as 'ghost cats' over a **BroadcastChannel**. There's also a Konami code, a desk-warping mode, and small `localStorage` counters tracking what you've done.

## Why build it this way

No build step, no dependencies, and it still loads fast. Most of the fun is hidden on purpose, so you only really find it by poking around.

title: GameChangineer
description:
**GameChangineer** is an educational platform from **Virginia Tech's ECE department** that lets students build real, playable games by describing them in plain English. Type something like 'make the cat jump when I press space, and lose if a fox touches it,' and the platform turns that sentence into a working game, with no syntax to memorize and no blocks to drag.

## The bigger idea

The goal is to teach what Virginia Tech calls 'AI-native' skills: describing what you want to a model clearly, then judging for yourself whether what comes back is actually what you meant. A student writes the rules in plain language and the platform builds a running game with sprites, movement, collisions, scoring, and win/lose conditions, so a first playable game can be one sentence away. It runs entirely in the browser behind a Google sign-in with no install, and it's used in classrooms and **Hour of AI / Code** events.

## Under the hood

An **LLM** reads the natural-language description and generates the game logic, which then runs as a playable 2D game in the browser. Because the loop goes straight from a written prompt to a game you can play, students get a lot of practice phrasing a request well.

## What I worked on

I playtested and gave feedback: building games the way a student would, finding where the natural-language interpretation broke or surprised me, and passing along what felt confusing so the team could tighten it up.

title: Codetations / Magic Markup
description:
**Codetations** (also called Magic Markup) takes on a frustrating problem: notes you attach to code, like a comment, a proof, or a code-review remark, tend to break the moment the surrounding code changes. Codetations keeps each annotation pinned to the right code as the file evolves, instead of letting it drift to the wrong line after the next edit. It grew out of research on robust metadata anchoring for source code and ships as a **VS Code extension** for 'rich code annotations.'

## Keeping a note anchored

The system splits into a few pieces. A **document server** streams the live file over a **WebSocket**, a **state server** keeps a JSON file where each annotation is stored on its own alongside the text it was anchored to, and a stateless **retagging function** re-locates every annotation whenever the document changes, calling an **LLM** to re-anchor when the original text is no longer an exact match. A note placed on line 5 still lands on the right code after lines above it are added, removed, or rewritten.

## The tech stack

The extension is **TypeScript** on the **VS Code API**, with an **Express** and **WebSocket** backend for the document and state servers and `chokidar` watching files for changes. Retagging calls the **OpenAI API**. The annotation panel is a **React 18** webview built with **Vite**, using `react-markdown` and a TipTap rich-text editor to render notes, and it hooks into **GitHub Copilot Chat** as an extension dependency.

## What I contributed

I worked on the extension's **webview UI**, fixing rendering bugs in the annotation tools and reworking the **Annotation Generator** so it handles **Markdown** properly, which got the panel that creates and shows annotations behaving correctly.
